# Sources and scholarly provenance {#sec-source-provenance}

```{=html}
<span id="sec-p2-d-provenance" class="legacy-anchor" aria-hidden="true"></span>
```

We develop the reporting problem and its relation to earlier work from selected primary sources, which also inform our interpretation of the illustrations. The review is selective across the fields concerned with ranking, multicriteria decisions and uncertainty. The bibliography lists the cited works; the text identifies the results and implementations examined. Precise passage locators remain in the supporting source records, while reader citations use author and year.

## Support for individual claims {#what-a-citation-supports}

```{=html}
<span id="what-the-original-passages-support" class="legacy-anchor" aria-hidden="true"></span>
```

We use source passages to identify a method's target, action, loss, assumptions and results, or to describe an institutional procedure. Applying a method to the present problem also requires comparison of the decision, available information and interpretation of the output. For example, rank intervals, selected subsets, predefined classes and common ordered grades are different reports even though all may be discussed in terms of ranking.

We used search records, bibliographic databases, citation links and summaries to locate works and alternative formulations. Substantive attribution rests on the primary passages examined in the specified editions. We examined selected sections and theorem statements without verifying every source proof, and retain the qualifications that distinguish a source guarantee from its application here.

## Editions and dated institutional descriptions

The cited version matters when pagination, assumptions, or claims differ. The preference discussion uses the 1993 Cambridge print edition of Keeney and Raiffa. Its publication history identifies the earlier 1976 Wiley edition; we have not compared the two editions line by line [@keeney_raiffa_1993]. The measurement discussion uses the inspected reproduction of Messick's 1994 research report, rather than a later journal version [@messick_validity_report_1994]. Likewise, the Bayesian multiple-comparison discussion uses the July 2006 working paper by Müller et al. [@MullerParmigianiRice2006]. The concepts and supporting passage records refer to these texts; broader questions of interpretation remain open.

Source versions also matter for mathematical attribution. The selected Markov-chain concentration statement in @sec-dependent-monte-carlo uses Paulin's corrected 2018 arXiv version 5, including the qualifications attached to its stationary reversible-chain result [@paulin_concentration_2018v5]. For multivariate output analysis, we use the asymptotic conditions stated in the published 2019 article; we do not certify its supplementary proofs or treat its stopping result as a finite-sample coordinate guarantee [@vats_multivariate_2019]. The descriptive allocation in @sec-descriptive-decomposition cites Shapley's dated 1952 RAND report. We give the permutation argument explicitly without applying the source's axiomatic uniqueness result or claiming a separate examination of the 1953 chapter [@shapley1952value].

Institutional descriptions refer to the dated materials cited. Hospital stars refer to the specified 2026 methodology, including the distinction between its scoring rules and policy restrictions [@CMSHospitalStars2026]. For Head Start, we use the inspected regulatory snapshot for its stated date, without assuming continuing currency, and distinguish it from earlier final-rule material and a later proposal. We treat the proposal separately from adopted rules [@hhsHeadStartEligibilitySelection2026; @acfHeadStartFinalRule2024; @acfHeadStartProposedRule2026]. These documents describe the procedures but do not establish their effects. A comparator based on them may reproduce only part of the operational system.

## Inherited ideas and local arguments {#inherited-ideas-and-arguments-supplied-here}

We draw on established posterior expected-loss decision making and scalar coherent report cards. We derive the weighted-risk and criterion-mixture identities for the targets, common-grade family, directional-error convention, weights and withholding cost considered here. They are developments within existing Bayesian postprocessing and multicriteria decision analysis. Their correspondence with scalar grading holds when the probability law, equality convention and feasible domain match as specified in @sec-scalar-reduction.

For domain profiles, we likewise distinguish the reporting problem from results derived under its assumptions. The proofs cover reductions, information requirements, product-family conditions, scope effects, representation costs, direct-versus-allocated protection and numerical assurance. Finite calculations illustrate specified laws, while the proofs establish the general results. The iid arguments require stated conditions on report selection and sampling, with numerical failure probabilities separate from posterior protection budgets.

The arguments and their assumptions are collected in @sec-proofs. We distinguish derived identities and sufficient conditions from chosen reporting objectives and numerical illustrations. For example, equal numerical coefficients do not make the co-primary composite and criterion-direction targets identical, and conditional optimality under one loss and evaluation law does not establish superiority under another. The relation to earlier work is discussed in @sec-synthesis-inheritance. Priority for the combined framework remains undetermined.

## Empirical and software boundaries

The KRW account uses selected passages of the published 2024 paper and the identified online appendix for the study frame, targets, producer, and source-specific numerical discussion [@kline_discrimination_2024]. In the historical reassessment we evaluate two reconstructed actions under identified coefficient conventions. We have not reproduced the original estimation procedure, established complete identity with its original-run inputs or added an empirical fit. These limitations are described in @sec-krw-reuse-interpretation.

The retained historical software correspondence in @sec-package-historical-record is based on a frozen 79-file inventory and one small evaluation. Later files carrying the same package version label lie outside that inventory. The current interface and reproduction records in @sec-package-current-interfaces and @sec-package-current-reproduction separately identify the inspected postrank 1.2.0 source, loaded library, supported decisions and executed examples, including the multidomain route. File fingerprints distinguish these source versions by byte identity. They provide no evidence about statistical calibration or algorithms that have not been examined. The exact synthetic checks, historical reuse and portable example archive are described in @sec-reproduction.

The four substantive case chapters use their identified existing analyses and saved results. The source versions, populations, target orientations, loss conventions and computational qualifications differ across Alabama, the Opportunity Atlas, PISA and California. Their inclusion does not claim a new model fit or a joint-profile reanalysis of all four datasets. The fictional 40-site example instead replays stored selections and diagnostic blocks under its specified synthetic design. Its dependent-chain frequencies remain distinct from conditional iid assurance.

The earlier profile literature audit is retained in a [17-source index](../assets/provenance/profile-audit/source-index.csv) and [71-row claim–source map](../assets/provenance/profile-audit/claim-source-map.csv), including precise locators and historical reading statuses. These dated records cover the sources examined; they are neither a complete bibliography nor a record of checking every cited proof. The [historical theorem ledger](../assets/provenance/profile-audit/theorem-ledger.csv) records formal assumptions and proof status. The complete arguments used in the current exposition appear in @sec-proofs.

Those source comparisons preserve several boundaries. Scalar report-card loss and its tie assumptions differ from the weak-error convention. Posterior ordering events, expected false-discovery fractions, repeated-sample rank coverage and future-ranking coverage protect different objects under different laws. A latent clustering credible set is not a grade-profile cell, and an unasserted direction is not an asserted equality. The relevant primary-source comparisons are developed in @sec-uncertainty-ordering, @sec-selection-benchmarks and @sec-profile-report-action.

Its exact coarsening example and its frequencies on stored fictional-site chains therefore carry different interpretations. Reproduction directions and their historical scope are retained in @sec-reproduction.

The uses and limits of these forms of evidence are summarized in @fig-vis-fc.

Evidence types and the scope of the claims they support. Primary passages support edition-specific attribution; local derivations support conclusions under their stated assumptions; exact finite checks address their declared laws and actions; fingerprints identify bytes; and dated execution records identify what was run. Each form of evidence also has its own limits. File identity does not establish scientific correctness, and finite calculations or successful runs do not prove a general theorem or model calibration. No row supplies evidence of unperformed empirical work.
:::

## Provenance of the equality-neutral extension {#sec-tie-aware-provenance}

We developed the equality-neutral branch from the project's structural-tie decision specification and compared it with the separate tie-aware software domain. Its statewise loss identities, guarded-minimizer proof, estimand comparison, finite-family frontier and perturbation arguments are derived in the main text under their stated conditions. The scalar ranking antecedent retains its original assumptions in @sec-krw-scalar-core and @sec-tie-aware-loss.

The extension is supported by general proofs, finite arithmetic checks and dated software records, each serving a different purpose. The public finite-check program in @sec-tie-aware-reproduction uses specified laws and enumerated actions, independently of the package evaluator. The software table in @sec-package-tie-aware reflects selected source/help inspection, while the dated installation results in @sec-package-tie-aware-evidence are earlier execution records. Assessing the prevalence of structural ties in institutional data, the calibration of a fitted posterior and the consequences of a funding rule requires evidence beyond these checks.
